title: How I run architecture reviews that engineers actually find useful
excerpt: Most architecture reviews are either rubber-stamps or interrogations. Neither produces better systems.
body:
Most architecture reviews are either rubber-stamps or interrogations. The rubber-stamp review exists to satisfy a process requirement and produces no real signal. The interrogation review produces anxiety and defensiveness rather than better designs. Neither outcome is what you want.

The format I have settled on

I structure reviews around three explicit phases, and I tell presenters about this structure in advance so they can prepare for it rather than being surprised by it.

Understanding phase: Before any critique, I ask questions until I can explain the proposed design back to the presenter. This does two things: it ensures I am not critiquing a misunderstanding of the design, and it often surfaces unstated assumptions that the presenter has not made explicit because they are obvious to them.

Tradeoffs phase: I ask the presenter to articulate what was given up to achieve the design's properties. Every design choice is a tradeoff. If a presenter cannot articulate what was traded away, that is a signal that the tradeoffs were not consciously made.

Risk phase: I ask what could go wrong, and specifically what the presenter is most uncertain about. Uncertainty is not a weakness — it is information. A presenter who can identify the riskiest assumption in their design has given the review something useful to focus on.

What I never do

I never critique a design without first understanding it well enough to defend it. And I never leave a review without ensuring the presenter knows what they need to do next — whether that is a specific revision, a prototype, or a consultation with another team.
